title: The vowel signs
hook: a reader gets through the line, proud, and the teacher taps one tiny mark
tomorrow: and the little dots on top? what are they doing?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gutka: a small book of the daily prayers, wrapped in cloth and kept up high. Small book, big word. Open one, and the first thing you notice is how busy the letters are.
screen: `SMALL BOOK, BIG WORD.` → `HOW BUSY THE LETTERS ARE.`

segments.voice: A substitute teacher reads the roll and lands on a name with the wrong vowel. Everybody laughs. The kid corrects it, and it stings a little anyway: one sound off, and it's somebody else's name. Sunday morning, a gurdwara classroom. A girl reads the opening of the Japji out loud, a finger under the line. Aad sach, jugaad sach: true in the beginning, true through the ages. She gets through it, proud. Then the teacher taps one letter. There's a mark here. What's it doing? Under the last letter of sach hangs a tiny tail. She didn't say it. And she's about to find out she wasn't supposed to.
screen: `ONE SOUND OFF, SOMEONE ELSE'S NAME.` → `AAD SACH, JUGAAD SACH.` → `A TINY TAIL UNDER THE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Gurmukhi letters are mostly consonants, and each carries a quiet a inside it until a sign says otherwise. The signs are called laga matra, and they hang on the letters: above, below, beside. Three to start. Kanna, a standing stroke after the letter, stretches the sound to aa. Sihari, a curl that rises over the top, is written before its letter but heard after it: the eye goes one way, the voice the other. And aunkar, a little tail beneath, makes a u. Now the girl's mark. In sach, that tail is an aunkar. In the Granth's language, a sign at the end of a word often does grammar, the kind of work an ending like s does in English, and in many readings it's barely sounded, or not at all. So she read it well, and the teacher wanted her to see why. The sign was telling her about the word, not only about her mouth. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Gurmukhi on the page and the words Sikhs sing are tied together sign by sign. Move one small mark and a word can become another word, or take on another job. The Guru's words reach people as sound, and the signs keep that sound true from one reader to the next.
screen: `A QUIET A INSIDE EVERY LETTER.` · `KANNA, SIHARI, AUNKAR.` · `THE END MARK DOES GRAMMAR.` · `ONE SIGN, ANOTHER WORD.` · then, large: `THE SMALL SIGNS.`

segments.voice: Draw three signs by hand, on paper or with a fingertip on your palm: the standing stroke of kanna, the rising curl of sihari, the little tail of aunkar. Say each sound softly as you draw it: aa, i, u. Then breathe slowly and trace them once more, as if your hand were learning before your head does.
Laga matra: the vowel signs that hang on Gurmukhi letters, above, below and beside, giving each letter its sound. The third word of the year.
Your line: the small signs. They carry the sound from one reader to the next. Three of twenty, done.

screen: `DAY 1429 COUNTS.` → `READING THE GRANTH · 3 OF 20.` → `TOMORROW: AND THE LITTLE DOTS ON TOP? WHAT ARE THEY DOING?`

howItsDone: In Sikh families and gurdwara classes, learners study the Gurmukhi letters together with their vowel signs, sounding out each letter-and-sign pair, before they read Gurbani aloud.

fork.setup: at a family reading, your little cousin skips the tiny tail under the last letter of a word. an uncle frowns. what's the fair thing to say?
options: she slipped: every mark has to be voiced clearly, or the line doesn't count.
she may be right: an end mark often does grammar and is barely said. ask a teacher's ear.
it doesn't matter either way, since small marks never change a word.
fork.reveal: in sach, the aunkar at the end does grammar and in many readings is barely sounded. but small signs can change a word, which is why readers check with someone who knows.

notes: v3 story day: a gurdwara class scene (a girl reads aad sach, jugaad sach; the teacher taps the aunkar under sach), with the cliffhanger answered in the teach.

Claim to check: a word-final aunkar or sihari in Gurbani often marks grammar and 'in many readings is barely sounded, or not at all'. Reading conventions differ between schools (some sound a light vowel); the script says 'many readings' on purpose. Confirm the example ਸਚੁ (sach, Ang 1) and the wording.
Gurmukhi descriptions: each consonant carries an inherent a; kanna (ਾ) aa, sihari (ਿ) written before and heard after, aunkar (ੁ) u. Confirm.
Gurmukhi ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ, ਕੰਨਾ, ਸਿਹਾਰੀ, ਔਂਕੜ, ਜਪੁਜੀ, ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ and the sound-outs to be checked; ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ is also written ਲਗ ਮਾਤ੍ਰਾ in some primers.
